title: Figurative Language & Literary Devices
description: Mastering similes, metaphors, personification, hyperbole, alliteration, onomatopoeia, oxymoron, irony and more — how writers create vivid imagery.

notes.heading: Simile and Metaphor

illustration.alt: Diagram comparing simile and metaphor: a simile keeps two ideas separate and links them with 'like' or 'as', a metaphor merges them into one identity with 'is', and an extended metaphor sustains one comparison across a whole passage.
illustration.caption: A simile compares with 'like' or 'as', while a metaphor asserts identity — and an extended metaphor sustains that comparison across a passage.

notes.body: Simile: comparison using 'like' or 'as' ('Her smile was like sunshine'). Metaphor: direct comparison stating something IS something else ('Her smile was sunshine'). Metaphors feel more powerful because they assert identity rather than mere similarity. Extended metaphor: a metaphor developed over several sentences or throughout a text. Example: Shakespeare's 'All the world's a stage' speech extends the theatre metaphor across an entire passage. Dead metaphor: so common we no longer notice it ('the leg of a table,' 'time is running out'). Mixed metaphor: combining incompatible metaphors (avoid!): 'We'll burn that bridge when we come to it.'

notes.heading: Personification, Pathetic Fallacy and Zoomorphism
notes.body: Personification: giving human qualities to non-human things ('The wind whispered through the trees'). Pathetic fallacy: a specific type of personification where nature reflects human emotions — the weather mirrors the mood ('The storm raged as her anger grew'). This is NOT just any personification — it must reflect emotion. Zoomorphism: attributing animal characteristics to humans or objects ('He wolfed down his food'). Anthropomorphism: giving human form/characteristics to animals or gods (talking animals in fables, Greek gods with human personalities).

notes.heading: Hyperbole, Understatement and Litotes
notes.body: Hyperbole: deliberate exaggeration for emphasis or humour ('I've told you a million times,' 'This bag weighs a ton'). Understatement: deliberately making something seem less important than it is — the opposite of hyperbole. A soldier describing a terrible battle as 'a bit noisy' is understatement. Litotes: a form of understatement using double negatives ('She's not unkind' = she is kind; 'He's no fool' = he's smart). Effective for irony, modesty, or subtle emphasis. Meiosis: dismissive understatement ('It's just a scratch' for a deep wound).

notes.heading: Sound Devices: Alliteration, Assonance, Onomatopoeia
notes.body: Alliteration: repetition of initial consonant sounds ('Peter Piper picked,' 'furious, fast, and fatal'). Creates rhythm, emphasis, and memorability. Sibilance: a specific type — repetition of 's' sounds ('The snake slithered silently') — creates a hissing, sinister effect. Assonance: repetition of vowel sounds within words ('The rain in Spain stays mainly in the plain'). Creates internal rhythm and musicality. Consonance: repetition of consonant sounds anywhere in words (not just initial). Onomatopoeia: words that imitate sounds ('buzz,' 'crash,' 'sizzle,' 'whisper,' 'clang'). Creates sensory immersion — the reader 'hears' the scene.

notes.heading: Oxymoron, Paradox and Juxtaposition
notes.body: Oxymoron: two contradictory words placed together ('bittersweet,' 'deafening silence,' 'living death,' 'organised chaos'). Creates tension and forces the reader to think. Paradox: a statement that seems self-contradictory but contains a deeper truth ('The more you learn, the more you realise you don't know,' 'I must be cruel to be kind'). Juxtaposition: placing two contrasting ideas, characters, or images side by side to highlight their differences. Dickens opens A Tale of Two Cities with: 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times' — juxtaposing extremes to capture an era's contradictions.

notes.heading: Irony: Verbal, Situational and Dramatic
notes.body: Verbal irony: saying the opposite of what you mean (sarcasm's sophisticated cousin). 'What a beautiful day!' during a hurricane. Situational irony: when the outcome is the opposite of what was expected. A fire station burning down. A pilot afraid of heights. Dramatic irony: when the audience knows something characters don't — creating tension. In Romeo and Juliet, we know Juliet is not dead, but Romeo does not — we watch helplessly as he makes his fatal decision. Irony adds layers of meaning and engages the reader in actively interpreting the text.

notes.heading: Analysing Figurative Language
notes.body: When analysing figurative language, don't just IDENTIFY the technique — explain its EFFECT. Wrong: 'The author uses a simile.' Right: 'The author's simile comparing the abandoned house to 'a skull with empty eye sockets' creates an unsettling, death-haunted atmosphere that foreshadows the discovery within.' Questions to ask: Why this particular comparison? What connotations do these words carry? How does this device affect the reader's emotions? What would be lost if the author wrote literally instead? Always treat figurative language as a deliberate choice — authors could have written literally but chose imagery for a specific effect.
